results.note: p. 4 of the online-first PDF (PDF page 5), Cardiac complications. 1st paragraph: Turnipseed et al. (2003), 9 (25%) of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients with acute coronary syndrome (heart rate 114 against 98 per minute). 2nd paragraph: Hawley et al. (2013) systolic 148 mm Hg (95% CI 144, 152), diastolic 86 (83, 89), heart rate 116 (97.3, 134.7), 3 episodes of ventricular tachycardia and 15 of cardiac ischaemia with no denominator; Fatovich et al. (2012) tachycardia 42%, hypertension 6.4%; Lan et al. (1998) 85% and 69%. Every number matches; nothing is pooled; role supports fits the statement's study-level list. The review's sentence could also be read as 9 of 36 methamphetamine-positive patients having both chest pain and the syndrome; the anchor's reading (36 chest-pain patients) agrees with Table 1, which describes Turnipseed's series as patients with chest pain, and the 36-against-171 discrepancy is carried by anchor 3.

Table 1 read on the rotated rendered pp. 5–6: Gray et al. (2007)/Fatovich et al. (2012) row (self-reported amphetamine-related presentations, Perth) agitated delirium 20%, psychosis 12%, suicidal thoughts 6%; Cloutier/Hendrickson row suicidal 25%, psychotic 12%; Bunting et al. (2007) aggression 18%; Lan et al. (1998) suicide attempts 50%, all 44 methamphetamine-positive; Pasic et al. (2007) psychosis 80%, suicidal 40%, agitation 13%; Szuster (1990) aggression 50%, paranoid 86%; Toles et al. (2006) agitation 48%, suicidal 47%. p. 7, Behavioural and psychiatric problems: 1st paragraph (aggression, police) and 2nd paragraph (Pasic, 48 (80%) of 60 acutely psychotic). All match; role supports fits. The Cloutier row is shared with two Hendrickson papers; attributing its percentages to Cloutier's psychiatric visits is the natural reading.

corrected.extracted: The review could not pool any clinical feature: the studies had no consistent measures of clinical characteristics, so its meta-analyses were limited to sex, age and the share of methamphetamine-positive attendees. Its inclusion criteria admitted studies of methamphetamine and related amphetamines (p. 2). The authors list problems with the chart reviews in identifying use, its pattern and frequency, the type of methamphetamine and other drug use, and with self-report; three included studies counted cocaine or other stimulant use; positive urine toxicology likely includes other amphetamine-like compounds and stays positive for 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use to the presentation; time of last use was not accurately assessed. Two sets of included studies are linked to the same data, and Table 1 lists the acute coronary syndrome study with 171 subjects, against 36 in the text. No deaths or case fatality are reported anywhere in the review's results.

results.note: Every element is at the stated places: p. 2 Selection criteria (one paragraph; inclusion of 'related amphetamines'); p. 4 Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph (amphetamine-like compounds) and 3rd paragraph (two linked sets, plus a 20-year repeat at one unit); p. 6 Table 1, Turnipseed row (all 171 methamphetamine-positive); p. 10 Critical reflection (a single paragraph). The quotation is verbatim (8 words, p. 10). Two wording fixes: the source speaks of a lack of accurate assessment of time of last use, not that it was not recorded, and says the 72-hour window makes it difficult to link use accurately to the presentation; and the p. 2 locator carried no content in the extracted text, so its point is added. No deaths: confirmed for Results and Table 1 (the nearest item is Hawley's 'life-threatening complication 9%'); deaths appear only in the Introduction, cited from other sources. Role qualifies fits.

p. 137: 2007 NSMHWB, 8,841, stratified multistage household probability sample aged 16–85, response 60%, stimulant subsample 579 with valid age of first use (2.1, 1st paragraph); criteria asked only of people who used a drug at least five times (2.1, 2nd paragraph); modified WMH-CIDI 3.0, lifetime DSM-IV abuse or dependence (2.2, 1st paragraph). p. 138: conditional probabilities are descriptive estimates (2.3, 1st paragraph); stimulants 45.7% (39.5–51.8), median onset age 20 (IQR 18–24) (3.2.1, 3rd paragraph). No drug is named in the stimulant class anywhere in the text (searched). All match. Role qualifies is acceptable; since the statement now reports these figures, supports would also fit.

corrected.locator: Results › 3.1, 2nd paragraph, and Methods › 2.7, 3rd paragraph (p. 3); Table 3 and Results › 3.4. Dose-response profile, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
corrected.extracted: Heaviest frequency of use at ages 18–35: never 751 (71.9%), once or twice 124 (11.9%), up to about monthly 118 (11.3%), at least weekly 51 (4.9%). The outcome is violence at any time from 18 to 35, so the heaviest use and the violence need not fall in the same period. Odds ratios against never, adjusted only for a reduced set of fixed childhood and adolescent confounders (those significant in Model 1: family socioeconomic status, sex, child IQ, adolescent anxiety disorder, childhood physical and sexual abuse, deviant peers, attention problems), not for the time-varying covariates of Model 2: violence perpetration 1.13 (0.64–2.02), 1.40 (0.81–2.42) and 4.84 (2.48–9.46); victimisation 1.87 (1.13–3.11), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 3.62 (1.88–6.96); intimate-partner perpetration 1.75 (1.05–2.90), 1.89 (1.15–3.11) and 2.44 (1.26–4.71); intimate-partner victimisation 1.12 (0.72–1.74), 1.45 (0.95–2.22) and 2.28 (1.24–4.19). The methods say categories were compared pairwise, but only comparisons with never are reported.

results.note: All counts, percentages and the twelve odds ratios with intervals match 3.1 (p. 3) and Table 3 (rendered p. 5); 751+124+118+51 = 1,044. Two precisions: Table 3 is adjusted for the subset of Model 1 confounders listed in 3.4 (including two adolescent factors), not for 'childhood confounders' in general; and Methods 2.7 (3rd paragraph, p. 3) defines the outcome as lifetime (18–35) violence against the maximum frequency in any period, which matters for reading the gradient. The pairwise tests that 2.7 describes are not reported. Role qualifies fits.

corrected.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (p. 1, quotation); Methods › 2.6, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 2, note d (p. 4); Results › 3.5. Comparison with ecstasy exposure (p. 5); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 5) and 5th paragraph (pp. 5–6)
corrected.extracted: The authors conclude that methamphetamine use is an independent risk factor for violence, but state that they could not be sure of the order of use and violence within each interview period, which limited causal inference; that use and violence were self-reported and not corroborated; and that most people who used did not engage in or experience violence. Of other substances, only alcohol and cannabis use disorders were adjusted for, not other illicit drug use. Ecstasy, analysed the same way, showed no statistically significant adjusted association with any of the four outcomes (all p > 0.05; the authors call the evidence inconclusive); its estimates are only in a supplement.

results.note: Quotation verbatim from the abstract's Conclusions (12 words; the changelog says 11). Discussion 2nd paragraph (p. 5): causal and temporal order unknown, most people who used did not engage in or experience violence; 5th paragraph (pp. 5–6): temporal order within periods unknown, which limited causal inference, self-report, violence not corroborated. Correction 1: the paper reports 'inconclusive evidence of associations (all p values > 0.05)' for ecstasy, which is absence of evidence, not 'no adjusted association'. Correction 2: the statement about the adjustment set comes from Methods 2.6 (p. 3) and Table 2 note d (p. 4), which the locator did not name. Role qualifies fits.
